items.stem: Which equation is used to calculate average speed?
options: average speed = total time ÷ total distance
average speed = (first speed + last speed) ÷ 2 always
average speed = total distance ÷ total time
items.answer: average speed = total distance ÷ total time
items.markingKey: v = s/t using totals for the whole journey.

items.stem: Explain why the average speed for a whole journey is not usually equal to the mean of the speeds on each part.
items.answer: The parts usually take different times; average speed = total distance ÷ total time, so slower parts (which last longer) count more.
items.markingKey: definition with totals [1]; parts take different times [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how to measure the average speed of a cyclist using equipment in a school.
items.answer: Measure a distance along the road with a tape (e.g. 100 m); time the cyclist over it with a stopwatch; speed = distance ÷ time; repeat and average.
items.markingKey: measure distance with tape [1]; time with stopwatch [1]; v = s/t [1] [3]

items.stem: A tortoise crawls 7 m in 25 min. Work out the average speed in m/min.
items.answer: 0.28 m/min
items.markingKey: v = s/t = 7/25 = 0.28 m/min. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Kenji cycles to school 4 km in 25 min. Calculate the average speed in m/s.

A courier in Cairo jogs 1.2 km in 6 min, waits 5 min at a crossing, then cycles 6.0 km in 15 min. (a) Calculate the average speed for the whole journey in m/s. (b) State one reason why the journey has a velocity that changes even if the speed were steady.
items.answer: (a) 4.62 m/s (b) The direction of travel changes (turns in the road), and velocity is a vector.
items.markingKey: (a) total distance 7200 m [1]; total time 1560 s [1]; = 4.62 m/s [1] [3] (b) The direction of travel changes (turns in the road), and velocity is a vector [1]

items.stem: What is the SI unit of speed?
items.answer: m/s
items.markingKey: Metres per second.

items.stem: Two cars travel at 50 km/h, one north and one south. Explain whether they have the same speed and the same velocity.
items.answer: Same speed (50 km/h) but different velocities because they move in different directions.
items.markingKey: same speed [1]; velocity differs due to direction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why light gates connected to a timer give a more accurate speed than a hand-held stopwatch.
items.answer: Light gates start and stop the timer automatically, removing human reaction-time error, and can time very short intervals.
items.markingKey: no reaction time [1]; short intervals measured precisely [1] [2]

items.stem: A swimmer swims 400 m in 309 s. What is the average speed in m/s?
A rowing boat moves at a constant speed of 15 m/s for 20 s. Determine the distance travelled.
items.markingKey: s = vt = 15 × 20 = 300 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Leila travels to a market in Mumbai: walks 2.4 km in 10 min, waits 8 min for a bus, then rides 3.6 km in 9 min. (a) Calculate the average speed for the first stage in m/s. (b) Explain the difference between the speed shown on the bus speedometer and the average speed for the bus ride.
items.answer: (a) 4 m/s (b) The speedometer shows instantaneous speed at each moment; the average is total distance ÷ total time, including speeding up and slowing down.
items.markingKey: (a) 2400 m / 600 s = 4 m/s (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) The speedometer shows instantaneous speed at each moment [1]; the average is total distance ÷ total time, including speeding up and slowing down [1] [2]

items.stem: On a distance-time graph, what does a horizontal line show?
items.answer: The object is stationary
items.markingKey: Distance not changing → at rest.

items.stem: Explain why a distance-time graph can never slope downwards, but a displacement-time graph can.
items.answer: Distance travelled can only increase or stay the same; displacement is measured from the start and can decrease when the object comes back.
items.markingKey: distance never decreases [1]; displacement can return towards start [1] [2]

items.stem: Two runners start together. On a distance-time graph, runner A’s line is steeper than runner B’s. Explain what this shows and who wins a race of fixed length.
items.answer: A has the greater speed (bigger gradient), so A covers the fixed distance in less time and wins.
items.markingKey: steeper = faster [1]; A wins [1] [2]

items.stem: The distance-time graph for a model train is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (15 s, 90 m), (30 s, 90 m), (40 s, 150 m). Calculate the speed during the first section.
items.answer: 6 m/s
items.markingKey: gradient = 90/15 = 6 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The distance-time graph for a ferry is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (20 s, 120 m), (35 s, 120 m), (45 s, 320 m). Describe the motion in each section and calculate the speed in the last section.
items.answer: Constant speed 6 m/s; stationary for 15 s; constant speed 20 m/s.
items.markingKey: section 1 constant speed [1]; section 2 stationary [1]; last section gradient = 200/10 = 20 m/s [1] [3]

items.stem: The distance-time graph for a cyclist is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (40 s, 200 m), (55 s, 200 m), (75 s, 260 m). (a) Calculate the speed in the first and last sections. (b) Calculate the average speed for the whole motion. (c) State in which section the object was fastest and explain how the graph shows this.
items.answer: (a) 5 m/s and 3 m/s (b) 3.47 m/s (c) first section: steepest gradient.
items.markingKey: (a) 5 m/s and 3 m/s [2] (b) 260/75 = 3.47 m/s [1] (c) steepest gradient [1] [4]

items.stem: A distance-time graph for a delivery van is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (40 s, 200 m), (55 s, 200 m), (65 s, 400 m). (a) Calculate the speed in the last section. (b) In reality the changes in speed are not instant. Describe how the graph would really look at the corners.
items.answer: (a) 20 m/s (b) The corners would be smooth curves, showing the object speeding up or slowing down gradually.
items.markingKey: (a) (400 − 200)/(65 − 55) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 20 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) curved corners [1]; gradual change of speed [1] [2]

items.stem: A distance-time graph for a model train is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (30 s, 150 m), (50 s, 150 m), (80 s, 200 m). (a) Describe the motion between 30 s and 50 s. (b) Calculate the speed in the last section. (c) In reality the changes in speed are not instant. Describe how the graph would really look at the corners.
items.answer: (a) Stationary (distance constant). (b) 1.67 m/s (c) The corners would be smooth curves, showing the object speeding up or slowing down gradually.
items.markingKey: (a) Stationary (distance constant) [1] (b) (200 − 150)/(80 − 50) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.67 m/s with unit [1] [2] (c) curved corners [1]; gradual change of speed [1] [2]

items.stem: On a distance-time graph, what does the gradient represent?
items.answer: Speed
items.markingKey: Gradient = Δdistance/Δtime = speed.

items.stem: A straight, sloping line on a distance-time graph shows …
items.answer: constant speed
items.markingKey: Constant gradient → constant speed.

items.stem: Explain how a distance-time graph shows that a car is slowing down.
items.answer: The gradient (slope) decreases with time: the curve becomes less steep, flattening out.
items.markingKey: gradient = speed [1]; decreasing gradient / flattening [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the shape of the distance-time graph for a ball thrown up a short distance, falling back, considering total distance travelled.
items.answer: The line rises with decreasing gradient to the top (slowing), then continues rising with increasing gradient as it falls (speeding up); it never goes down.
items.markingKey: decreasing gradient up [1]; increasing gradient on way down [1]; always increasing [1] [3]

items.stem: Readings for a snail on a ruler: time/s = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; distance/mm = 0, 10, 20, 30, 44, 50. (a) Identify the anomalous reading. (b) Using the other readings, determine the speed. (c) Describe the shape of the distance-time graph you would draw.
items.answer: (a) 44 mm at 8 s (b) 5 mm/s (c) a straight line through the origin (constant speed).
items.markingKey: (a) anomaly identified [1] (b) gradient = 50/10 = 5 mm/s [2] (c) straight line through origin [1] [4]

items.stem: The distance-time graph for a jogger is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (10 s, 50 m), (25 s, 50 m), (45 s, 200 m). Determine the speed during the first section.
items.answer: 5 m/s
items.markingKey: gradient = 50/10 = 5 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Readings for a snail on a ruler: time/s = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; distance/mm = 0, 12, 19.2, 36, 48, 60. (a) Identify the anomalous reading. (b) Using the other readings, determine the speed. (c) Describe the shape of the distance-time graph you would draw.
items.answer: (a) 19.2 mm at 4 s (b) 6 mm/s (c) a straight line through the origin (constant speed).
items.markingKey: (a) anomaly identified [1] (b) gradient = 60/10 = 6 mm/s [2] (c) straight line through origin [1] [4]

items.stem: A distance-time graph for a lift moving up a tower in Bogotá is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (20 s, 80 m), (30 s, 80 m), (50 s, 130 m). (a) Calculate the speed in the last section. (b) In reality the changes in speed are not instant. Describe how the graph would really look at the corners. (c) Sketch-describe the speed-time graph for the same motion.
items.answer: (a) 2.5 m/s (b) The corners would be smooth curves, showing the object speeding up or slowing down gradually. (c) Horizontal line at 4 m/s, then at 0 from 20 s to 30 s, then horizontal at 2.5 m/s.
items.markingKey: (a) (130 − 80)/(50 − 30) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.5 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) curved corners [1]; gradual change of speed [1] [2] (c) three levels correct [1]; Horizontal line at 4 m/s, then at 0 from 20 s to 30 s, then horizontal at 2.5 m/s [1] [2]

items.stem: What does the gradient of a speed-time graph represent?
items.answer: Acceleration
items.markingKey: Gradient = Δv/Δt = acceleration.

items.stem: Explain how a speed-time graph shows that the acceleration of an object is decreasing.
items.answer: The line is curved with a decreasing gradient (becoming less steep).
items.markingKey: gradient = acceleration [1]; gradient decreasing [1] [2]

items.stem: A student says "a negative acceleration means the object is moving backwards". Explain why this is not necessarily true.
items.answer: Negative acceleration means the velocity is decreasing (deceleration) in the direction of motion; the object can still be moving forwards while slowing down.
items.markingKey: means slowing down [1]; can still move forward [1] [2]

items.stem: A bus travelling at 5 m/s speeds up to 7.5 m/s in 5 s. Determine the acceleration.
items.answer: 0.5 m/s²
items.markingKey: a = Δv/Δt = (7.5 − 5)/5 = 0.5 m/s². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A bus travelling at 15 m/s speeds up to 16 m/s in 2 s. Calculate the acceleration.
items.answer: 0.5 m/s²
items.markingKey: a = Δv/Δt = (16 − 15)/2 = 0.5 m/s². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [3]

items.stem: A motorbike travelling at 27 m/s slows down with a constant deceleration of 2.5 m/s². Calculate the time taken to stop and the braking distance.

A train accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 2 s, travels at constant speed for 15 s and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 10 s. (a) Calculate the acceleration in the first stage. (b) State the resultant force on the vehicle during the constant-speed stage and explain.
items.answer: (a) 6 m/s² (b) Zero: the speed is constant so there is no acceleration (forces balanced).
items.markingKey: (a) a = 12/2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6 m/s² with unit [1] [2] (b) zero [1]; no acceleration [1] [2]

items.stem: A motorbike accelerates uniformly from rest to 15 m/s in 8 s, travels at constant speed for 30 s and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 3 s. (a) Calculate the total distance travelled. (b) State the resultant force on the vehicle during the constant-speed stage and explain.
items.answer: (a) 533 m (b) Zero: the speed is constant so there is no acceleration (forces balanced).
items.markingKey: (a) areas of two triangles and a rectangle [1]; total [2] [3] (b) zero [1]; no acceleration [1] [2]

items.stem: What does the area under a speed-time graph represent?
items.answer: Distance travelled
items.markingKey: Area = speed × time = distance.

items.stem: Explain why the distance travelled by a car that accelerates uniformly from rest is half of speed × time.
items.answer: The area under the speed-time graph is a triangle: ½ × base × height = ½ × t × v.
items.markingKey: area under graph = distance [1]; triangle area ½vt [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the motion shown by a speed-time graph that rises steeply, levels off, then falls to zero.
items.answer: The object accelerates from rest, travels at constant speed, then decelerates to a stop.
items.markingKey: accelerates [1]; constant speed [1]; decelerates to rest [1] [3]

items.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 18 m/s in 6 s. Sipho calculates the distance travelled as 18 × 6 = 108 m. Explain the mistake and give the correct distance.
items.answer: Sipho used the area of a rectangle; the speed was not 18 m/s throughout. Area of triangle = ½ × 6 × 18 = 54 m.
items.markingKey: identifies rectangle instead of triangle / average speed is 9 m/s [1]; correct 54 m [1] [2]

items.stem: A cyclist accelerates uniformly from rest to 15 m/s in 2 s, travels at 15 m/s for 30 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 3 s. Calculate the distance travelled while accelerating.
items.markingKey: area = ½ × 2 × 15 = 15 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A tram accelerates uniformly from rest to 15 m/s in 2 s, travels at 15 m/s for 10 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 10 s. Use the speed-time graph to calculate the total distance travelled.
items.markingKey: triangles ½×2×15 + ½×10×15 [1]; rectangle 10×15 [1]; total 240 m [1] [3]

items.stem: A cyclist accelerates uniformly from rest to 10 m/s in 5 s, travels at constant speed for 10 s and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 5 s. (a) Calculate the average speed for the whole journey. (b) Describe how the graph would differ if the deceleration were not uniform but became less as the vehicle slowed.
items.answer: (a) 7.5 m/s (b) The last section would be a curve that becomes less steep as it approaches zero speed.
items.markingKey: (a) 150/20 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 7.5 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) curve [1]; decreasing gradient [1] [2]

items.stem: A motorbike accelerates uniformly from rest to 6 m/s in 4 s, travels at constant speed for 20 s and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 4 s. (a) Calculate the acceleration in the first stage. (b) State the resultant force on the vehicle during the constant-speed stage and explain. (c) Describe how the graph would differ if the deceleration were not uniform but became less as the vehicle slowed.
items.answer: (a) 1.5 m/s² (b) Zero: the speed is constant so there is no acceleration (forces balanced). (c) The last section would be a curve that becomes less steep as it approaches zero speed.
items.markingKey: (a) a = 6/4 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.5 m/s² with unit [1] [2] (b) zero [1]; no acceleration [1] [2] (c) curve [1]; decreasing gradient [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the approximate acceleration of free fall near the Earth’s surface?
items.answer: 9.8 m/s²
items.markingKey: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (often rounded to 10 m/s²).

items.stem: Explain why, in air, a sheet of paper falls more slowly than the same sheet crumpled into a ball.
items.answer: The flat sheet has a larger surface area, so it experiences more air resistance; its resultant force and acceleration are smaller.
items.markingKey: larger area → more air resistance [1]; smaller resultant force / acceleration [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe an experiment to measure g using a falling ball and light gates.
items.answer: Drop a ball from rest through two light gates a measured distance apart; the timer records the speeds at each gate and the time between them; g = change in speed ÷ time.
items.markingKey: drop from rest through light gates [1]; measure speeds and time [1]; g = Δv/Δt [1] [3]

items.stem: A dropped key is dropped from rest near the Earth’s surface and falls freely for 2.5 s (g = 9.8 m/s²). Work out the speed reached.
items.markingKey: v = gt = 9.8 × 2.5 = 24.5 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A small steel ball is dropped from rest on Mars, where g = 3.7 m/s². Calculate its speed after 1 s and the distance it has fallen (use the area under the speed-time graph).
Consider a stone dropped down a deep well. (a) Describe how the graph changes when air resistance is significant. (b) State the acceleration at the start of the fall and explain.
items.answer: (a) The gradient decreases as speed increases; the curve levels off at terminal velocity. (b) 9.8 m/s²: at the start speed is zero, so air resistance is zero and only weight acts.
items.markingKey: (a) decreasing gradient [1]; levels off [1] [2] (b) g [1]; no air resistance at v = 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the acceleration of a dropped heavy ball is the same as that of a light ball (ignoring air resistance).
items.answer: The heavier ball has a larger weight but also a larger mass; a = W/m = g for both.
items.markingKey: larger weight and mass in proportion [1]; a = W/m = g [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a ball thrown upwards has an acceleration of 9.8 m/s² downwards even at the very top of its flight.
items.answer: At the top its velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity (its weight) still acts, so it still accelerates downwards at g.
items.markingKey: weight still acts [1]; acceleration is g downwards even when v = 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: In an experiment, Diego drops a card through two light gates. The speed at the upper gate is 1.14 m/s, the speed at the lower gate is 3.45 m/s and the time between gates is 0.25 s. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (b) Suggest why the value is not exactly 9.8 m/s².
items.answer: (a) 9.24 m/s² (b) air resistance on the card acts upwards, reducing the resultant force and so the acceleration (also timing/measurement uncertainty).
items.markingKey: (a) a = (3.45 − 1.14)/0.25 [1] = 9.24 m/s² [1] (b) air resistance or uncertainty [1] [3]

items.stem: In an experiment, Chloe drops a card through two light gates. The speed at the upper gate is 0.95 m/s, the speed at the lower gate is 3.8 m/s and the time between gates is 0.3 s. (a) Calculate the acceleration. (b) Suggest why the value is not exactly 9.8 m/s².
items.answer: (a) 9.5 m/s² (b) air resistance on the card acts upwards, reducing the resultant force and so the acceleration (also timing/measurement uncertainty).
items.markingKey: (a) a = (3.8 − 0.95)/0.3 [1] = 9.5 m/s² [1] (b) air resistance or uncertainty [1] [3]

items.stem: Consider a ball dropped from a tall bridge in Dubai. (a) Calculate the speed after 4 s, ignoring air resistance. (b) Sketch-describe the speed-time graph if air resistance is ignored. (c) State the acceleration at the start of the fall and explain.
items.answer: (a) 39.2 m/s (b) A straight line through the origin with gradient 9.8 m/s². (c) 9.8 m/s²: at the start speed is zero, so air resistance is zero and only weight acts.
items.markingKey: (a) v = gt = 9.8 × 4 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 39.2 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) straight line from origin [1]; gradient g [1] [2] (c) g [1]; no air resistance at v = 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: Velocity differs from speed because velocity …
options: can only be used for cars
items.answer: includes direction
items.markingKey: Velocity is speed in a given direction (a vector).

items.stem: Felix drives 120 km at 90 km/h and then another 120 km at 100 km/h. Felix says the average speed is 95 km/h. Explain why this is wrong and calculate the correct average speed.
items.answer: The slower half takes longer, so it counts more; average = 240/(1.33 + 1.2) = 94.7 km/h.
items.markingKey: times are unequal [1]; times 1.33 h and 1.2 h [1]; average = total distance/total time = 94.7 km/h [1] [3]

items.stem: A ferry crosses a bay from Istanbul 17.5 km in 20 min. Calculate the average speed in km/min.
items.answer: 0.875 km/min
items.markingKey: v = s/t = 17.5/20 = 0.875 km/min. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A courier in Accra jogs 1.5 km in 5 min, waits 4 min at a crossing, then cycles 6.0 km in 15 min. (a) Calculate the average speed for the first stage in m/s. (b) Calculate the speed for the last stage in km/h.
items.answer: (a) 5 m/s (b) 24 km/h
items.markingKey: (a) 1500 m / 300 s = 5 m/s (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) 6.0 km / 0.25 h = 24 km/h (method/substitution) [1]; answer 24 km/h with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: A distance-time graph that curves upwards (gets steeper) shows an object that is …
items.answer: accelerating
items.markingKey: Increasing gradient → increasing speed.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a distance-time graph can never slope downwards, but a displacement-time graph can. (b) Two runners start together. On a distance-time graph, runner A’s line is steeper than runner B’s. Explain what this shows and who wins a race of fixed length.
items.answer: (a) Distance travelled can only increase or stay the same; displacement is measured from the start and can decrease when the object comes back. (b) A has the greater speed (bigger gradient), so A covers the fixed distance in less time and wins.
items.markingKey: (a) distance never decreases [1]; displacement can return towards start [1] [2] (b) steeper = faster [1]; A wins [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya and Ana walk along the same path. On a distance-time graph, Priya’s line is straight with gradient 8 m/s and Ana’s is straight with gradient 4 m/s; Ana starts 10 s later. Compare their motion and state who reaches a point 120 m along the path first.
items.answer: Both move at constant speed; Priya is faster. Times: Priya 15 s, Ana 40 s, so Priya arrives first.
items.markingKey: both constant speed [1]; compares speeds via gradient [1]; times calculated [1]; correct conclusion [1] [4]

items.stem: Readings for a bubble rising in a tube of oil: time/s = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25; distance/cm = 0, 25, 40, 75, 100, 125. (a) Identify the anomalous reading. (b) Using the other readings, determine the speed. (c) Describe the shape of the distance-time graph you would draw.
items.answer: (a) 40 cm at 10 s (b) 5 cm/s (c) a straight line through the origin (constant speed).
items.markingKey: (a) anomaly identified [1] (b) gradient = 125/25 = 5 cm/s [2] (c) straight line through origin [1] [4]

items.stem: The distance-time graph for a model train is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (40 s, 200 m), (50 s, 200 m), (75 s, 300 m). Describe the motion in each section and calculate the speed in the last section.
items.answer: Constant speed 5 m/s; stationary for 10 s; constant speed 4 m/s.
items.markingKey: section 1 constant speed [1]; section 2 stationary [1]; last section gradient = 100/25 = 4 m/s [1] [3]

items.stem: A distance-time graph for a lift moving up a tower in Dubai is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (30 s, 150 m), (50 s, 150 m), (60 s, 250 m). (a) Describe the motion between 30 s and 50 s. (b) Calculate the speed in the first section. (c) Calculate the average speed for the whole motion.
items.answer: (a) Stationary (distance constant). (b) 5 m/s (c) 4.17 m/s
items.markingKey: (a) Stationary (distance constant) [1] (b) gradient = 150/30 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5 m/s with unit [1] [2] (c) 250/60 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.17 m/s with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A line sloping downwards on a speed-time graph shows … (b) Define acceleration.
items.answer: (a) deceleration (b) The change in velocity per unit time (a = Δv/Δt).
items.markingKey: (a) Negative gradient → decreasing speed. (b) change of velocity [1] per unit time [1] [2]

items.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 30 m/s in 10 s. Mei calculates the distance travelled as 30 × 10 = 300 m. Explain the mistake and give the correct distance.
items.answer: Mei used the area of a rectangle; the speed was not 30 m/s throughout. Area of triangle = ½ × 10 × 30 = 150 m.
items.markingKey: identifies rectangle instead of triangle / average speed is 15 m/s [1]; correct 150 m [1] [2]

items.stem: A motorbike travelling at 10 m/s speeds up to 17.5 m/s in 5 s. Work out the acceleration.
items.answer: 1.5 m/s²
items.markingKey: a = Δv/Δt = (17.5 − 10)/5 = 1.5 m/s². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An electric scooter accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 2 s, travels at 12 m/s for 15 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 5 s. Calculate the distance travelled while accelerating.
items.markingKey: area = ½ × 2 × 12 = 12 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A cyclist starts from rest and reaches 6.4 m/s in 8 s. Calculate the acceleration.
items.answer: 0.8 m/s²
items.markingKey: a = Δv/Δt = (6.4 − 0)/8 = 0.8 m/s². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [3]

items.markingKey: (a) 6/10: 0.6 m/s² [1] (b) areas of two triangles and a rectangle [1]; total [2] [3] (c) 105/25 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.2 m/s with unit [1] [2]

items.answer: (a) The heavier ball has a larger weight but also a larger mass; a = W/m = g for both. (b) Drop a ball from rest through two light gates a measured distance apart; the timer records the speeds at each gate and the time between them; g = change in speed ÷ time.
items.markingKey: (a) larger weight and mass in proportion [1]; a = W/m = g [1] [2] (b) drop from rest through light gates [1]; measure speeds and time [1]; g = Δv/Δt [1] [3]

items.stem: Chloe drops a 0.1 kg steel ball and a 1 kg steel ball together from a height of 5 m and claims the 1 kg ball "must land first because it is heavier". Explain whether Chloe is correct, ignoring air resistance.
items.answer: Not correct: both fall with the same acceleration g = 9.8 m/s², because the larger weight acts on a proportionally larger mass (a = W/m = g), so they land together.
items.markingKey: land together [1]; same acceleration g [1]; weight ∝ mass so a = W/m = g [1] [3]

items.stem: A stone is dropped from rest near the Earth’s surface and falls freely for 1 s (g = 9.8 m/s²). Calculate the speed reached.
items.markingKey: v = gt = 9.8 × 1 = 9.8 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Consider a stone dropped down a deep well. (a) Calculate the speed after 2.5 s, ignoring air resistance. (b) Sketch-describe the speed-time graph if air resistance is ignored.
items.answer: (a) 24.5 m/s (b) A straight line through the origin with gradient 9.8 m/s².
items.markingKey: (a) v = gt = 9.8 × 2.5 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 24.5 m/s with unit [1] [2] (b) straight line from origin [1]; gradient g [1] [2]

items.stem: A speed of 36 km/h is the same as …
items.answer: 10 m/s

items.stem: Hana drives 60 km at 30 km/h and then another 60 km at 80 km/h. Hana says the average speed is 55 km/h. Explain why this is wrong and calculate the correct average speed.
items.answer: The slower half takes longer, so it counts more; average = 120/(2 + 0.75) = 43.6 km/h.
items.markingKey: times are unequal [1]; times 2 h and 0.75 h [1]; average = total distance/total time = 43.6 km/h [1] [3]

items.stem: A rowing boat moves at a constant speed of 15 m/s for 30 s. Calculate the distance travelled.
items.markingKey: s = vt = 15 × 30 = 450 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Freya travels to a market in Kuala Lumpur: walks 2.4 km in 10 min, waits 8 min for a bus, then rides 4.5 km in 15 min. (a) Calculate the average speed for the whole journey in m/s. (b) State one reason why the journey has a velocity that changes even if the speed were steady.
items.answer: (a) 3.48 m/s (b) The direction of travel changes (turns in the road), and velocity is a vector.
items.markingKey: (a) total distance 6900 m [1]; total time 1980 s [1]; = 3.48 m/s [1] [3] (b) The direction of travel changes (turns in the road), and velocity is a vector [1]

items.stem: On a distance-time graph, the steeper of two straight lines shows …
items.answer: the greater speed
items.markingKey: Larger gradient = larger speed.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how a distance-time graph shows that a car is slowing down. (b) Two runners start together. On a distance-time graph, runner A’s line is steeper than runner B’s. Explain what this shows and who wins a race of fixed length.
items.answer: (a) The gradient (slope) decreases with time: the curve becomes less steep, flattening out. (b) A has the greater speed (bigger gradient), so A covers the fixed distance in less time and wins.
items.markingKey: (a) gradient = speed [1]; decreasing gradient / flattening [1] [2] (b) steeper = faster [1]; A wins [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how a distance-time graph shows that a car is slowing down. (b) Explain why a distance-time graph can never slope downwards, but a displacement-time graph can.
items.answer: (a) The gradient (slope) decreases with time: the curve becomes less steep, flattening out. (b) Distance travelled can only increase or stay the same; displacement is measured from the start and can decrease when the object comes back.
items.markingKey: (a) gradient = speed [1]; decreasing gradient / flattening [1] [2] (b) distance never decreases [1]; displacement can return towards start [1] [2]

items.stem: Readings for a bubble rising in a tube of oil: time/s = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25; distance/cm = 0, 25, 50, 75, 110, 125. (a) Identify the anomalous reading. (b) Using the other readings, determine the speed. (c) Describe the shape of the distance-time graph you would draw.
items.answer: (a) 110 cm at 20 s (b) 5 cm/s (c) a straight line through the origin (constant speed).
items.markingKey: (a) anomaly identified [1] (b) gradient = 125/25 = 5 cm/s [2] (c) straight line through origin [1] [4]

items.stem: The distance-time graph for a model train is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (20 s, 80 m), (35 s, 80 m), (55 s, 280 m). Describe the motion in each section and calculate the speed in the last section.
items.answer: Constant speed 4 m/s; stationary for 15 s; constant speed 10 m/s.
items.markingKey: section 1 constant speed [1]; section 2 stationary [1]; last section gradient = 200/20 = 10 m/s [1] [3]

items.stem: A distance-time graph for a ferry is made of straight lines joining (0 s, 0 m), (15 s, 90 m), (25 s, 90 m), (55 s, 290 m). (a) Describe the motion between 15 s and 25 s. (b) Calculate the speed in the first section. (c) Sketch-describe the speed-time graph for the same motion.
items.answer: (a) Stationary (distance constant). (b) 6 m/s (c) Horizontal line at 6 m/s, then at 0 from 15 s to 25 s, then horizontal at 6.67 m/s.
items.markingKey: (a) Stationary (distance constant) [1] (b) gradient = 90/15 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6 m/s with unit [1] [2] (c) three levels correct [1]; Horizontal line at 6 m/s, then at 0 from 15 s to 25 s, then horizontal at 6.67 m/s [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Define acceleration. (b) What does the gradient of a speed-time graph represent?
items.answer: (a) The change in velocity per unit time (a = Δv/Δt). (b) Acceleration
items.markingKey: (a) change of velocity [1] per unit time [1] [2] (b) Gradient = Δv/Δt = acceleration.

items.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 24 m/s in 5 s. Yusuf calculates the distance travelled as 24 × 5 = 120 m. Explain the mistake and give the correct distance.
items.answer: Yusuf used the area of a rectangle; the speed was not 24 m/s throughout. Area of triangle = ½ × 5 × 24 = 60 m.
items.markingKey: identifies rectangle instead of triangle / average speed is 12 m/s [1]; correct 60 m [1] [2]

items.stem: A tram travelling at 5 m/s speeds up to 14.6 m/s in 12 s. Work out the acceleration.
items.answer: 0.8 m/s²
items.markingKey: a = Δv/Δt = (14.6 − 5)/12 = 0.8 m/s². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 24 m/s in 5 s, travels at 24 m/s for 10 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 10 s. Determine the distance travelled while accelerating.
items.markingKey: area = ½ × 5 × 24 = 60 m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An electric scooter accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 8 s, travels at 12 m/s for 20 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 6 s. Use the speed-time graph to calculate the total distance travelled.
items.markingKey: triangles ½×8×12 + ½×6×12 [1]; rectangle 20×12 [1]; total 324 m [1] [3]

items.stem: An electric scooter accelerates uniformly from rest to 6 m/s in 5 s, travels at constant speed for 15 s and then decelerates uniformly to rest in 6 s. (a) Calculate the acceleration in the first stage. (b) Calculate the average speed for the whole journey. (c) State the resultant force on the vehicle during the constant-speed stage and explain.
items.answer: (a) 1.2 m/s² (b) 4.73 m/s (c) Zero: the speed is constant so there is no acceleration (forces balanced).
items.markingKey: (a) a = 6/5 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.2 m/s² with unit [1] [2] (b) 123/26 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.73 m/s with unit [1] [2] (c) zero [1]; no acceleration [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a ball thrown upwards has an acceleration of 9.8 m/s² downwards even at the very top of its flight. (b) Describe an experiment to measure g using a falling ball and light gates.
items.answer: (a) At the top its velocity is momentarily zero, but gravity (its weight) still acts, so it still accelerates downwards at g. (b) Drop a ball from rest through two light gates a measured distance apart; the timer records the speeds at each gate and the time between them; g = change in speed ÷ time.
items.markingKey: (a) weight still acts [1]; acceleration is g downwards even when v = 0 [1] [2] (b) drop from rest through light gates [1]; measure speeds and time [1]; g = Δv/Δt [1] [3]

items.stem: A coin is dropped from a tall tower, ignoring air resistance. The time of fall is increased by 50%. Predict, with a reason, how the speed reached changes.
items.answer: The speed reached increases by 50%.
items.markingKey: Using v = gt: speed reached ∝ time of fall; factor = 1.50 = 1.50. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A tennis ball is dropped from rest near the Earth’s surface and falls freely for 0.5 s (g = 9.8 m/s²). Determine the speed reached.
items.markingKey: v = gt = 9.8 × 0.5 = 4.9 m/s. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Consider a parcel released from a hovering helicopter. (a) Calculate the distance fallen in 2 s. (b) Sketch-describe the speed-time graph if air resistance is ignored.
items.answer: (a) 19.6 m (b) A straight line through the origin with gradient 9.8 m/s².
items.markingKey: (a) area = ½ × 2 × 19.6 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 19.6 m with unit [1] [2] (b) straight line from origin [1]; gradient g [1] [2]
